I've farmed these lands in Quzhou County for over fifty years. The double-cropping system of winter wheat followed by summer maize is what I know, and at my age, I don't have the strength or the heart to experiment with new crops. My body isn't what it used to be—my back aches after a day in the fields—so I need a system that is predictable, doesn't require too much heavy labor, and gives me grain I can either eat or sell easily.

My wheat was sown last October on about 3 mu of land. I used an improved local variety—Shimai 22—which has served me well. I do rotary tillage before wheat sowing because the soil needs loosening after the maize stubble. For the wheat, I apply basal compound fertilizer and topdress with urea in spring. I irrigate four times: winter irrigation, green-up water, jointing water, and grain-filling water. I spray for insects two or three times and use herbicide once. I expect around 1000 jin per mu.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant summer maize—hybrid Denghai 605, which I buy from the seed dealer every year. I use no-tillage sowing because there's no time to plow between crops, and frankly, at 73, turning the soil twice a year is too much for me. Maize needs less fuss: two irrigations, usually at the jointing and filling stages, and about three pesticide applications for insects and weeds. I expect roughly 1100 jin per mu from the maize.

Some younger farmers are growing vegetables like chili or stevia for higher profits, but those crops need constant attention, more spraying, and tricky marketing. I'm too old for that risk. Wheat and maize prices are stable, the grain station buys them without haggling, and if the market is bad, I can store grain in my courtyard and eat it. That security matters more to me now than chasing higher profits.
